content: Tropical diseases are infectious diseases that either occur exclusively in tropical and subtropical regions, which is relatively rare, or are more prevalent in these areas and harder to prevent or control. With the advent of air travel, people increasingly visit these regions and contract many of these diseases, with malaria and hepatitis being among the most notable. However, it is crucial not to overlook non-tropical conditions in individuals returning from tropical regions. The Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR) of the World Health Organization focuses on neglected infectious diseases that disproportionately affect impoverished and marginalized populations in developing regions of the Americas, Asia, and Africa. The current portfolio of diseases under this program includes African trypanosomiasis, dengue fever, leishmaniasis, malaria, schistosomiasis, tuberculosis, Chagas disease, leprosy, lymphatic filariasis, and onchocerciasis. Although leprosy and tuberculosis are not exclusively tropical diseases, their highest incidence in tropical regions justifies their inclusion. Cholera and yellow fever also fall into this category. Some tropical diseases are exceedingly rare but can occur in sudden epidemics, such as Ebola hemorrhagic fever, Lassa fever, and Marburg virus. Additionally, there are hundreds of lesser-known or rarer tropical diseases that still hold significant public health importance. Examples include Oropouche virus, lobomycosis, West Nile disease, Lábrea fever, Rocio disease, Mapucho hemorrhagic fever, trachoma, Guinea worm disease, and chikungunya, among others. One of the primary reasons for the prevalence of tropical diseases is the hot climate present year-round in these regions, combined with higher volumes of rainfall. These factors contribute to the formation of breeding grounds for disease vectors, an increased number and variety of natural reservoirs, and zoonotic diseases that can be transmitted to humans. The abundance of insect vectors capable of transmitting diseases also plays a significant role. Furthermore, higher temperatures may facilitate the replication of pathogenic agents both within and outside biological organisms. Socioeconomic factors also contribute to the burden of tropical diseases, as many of the world's poorest nations are located in tropical regions. However, countries like Brazil, which have improved their socioeconomic conditions and invested in hygiene, public health, and the control of transmissible diseases, have achieved remarkable success in reducing or eliminating many endemic tropical diseases within their territories. The greenhouse effect and the rising global atmospheric temperatures appear to be influencing the spread of tropical diseases and their vectors to previously unaffected latitudes, such as the southern United States and the Mediterranean region.
